L20: At NC State College of Veterinary Medicine, some of the most important advances in veterinary medicine begin with the question--- Can we find a better way to help our patients? Our Clinical Trials Program allows our faculty, staff and trainees to tackle that question by moving our discoveries from the research lab to the clinic. A great example of this is Dr. 【12†Autumn Harris】 work on chronic kidney disease (CKD) in cats.
L21: CKD affects many older cats, and one of its complications is anemia, which can contribute to weakness, decreased appetite, reduced energy and a poorer quality of life. Our 【13†NC State College of Veterinary Medicine】 led by Drs. Harris and Vaden, is currently enrolling cats in a clinical trial evaluating an investigational treatment for anemia associated with CKD. The goal is to help advance the development of new treatment options for cats affected by both kidney disease and anemia.
L22: This is just one of the many clinical trials underway at the College. Studies are available across multiple species and veterinary specialties, and participation is not limited to current NC State Veterinary Hospital patients.🐱 Learn more about the feline CKD and anemia clinical trial: 【14†https://lnkd.in/gzrkmeyy】 Explore current NC State Veterinary Medicine clinical trials:【15†https://lnkd.in/grehcvyh】 【16†Joshua Stern】 【17†Shelly Vaden】 【18†Hyemi Sevening】

L45: Early but promising news for dogs with bone cancer. Researchers at The Ohio State University College of Veterinary Medicine tested an experimental drug, Telomir-Zn, on osteosarcoma cells from dogs and humans. In the lab, low doses slowed tumor-cell growth in all three cell lines tested. Osteosarcoma is one of the hardest diagnoses in veterinary oncology, especially for large-breed dogs, and treatment options are limited. The same disease also affects people.
L46: So research that could help both dogs and humans is worth watching. These are lab results only and haven't been peer reviewed yet. L63: The Feline Veterinary Medical Association (FelineVMA) has launched the Cat Friendly Resource Center, a free online hub to help veterinary practices reduce feline stress and bring more cats in for routine care. The Resource Center will provide: ✅ Quick tips and practical guides ✅ Printable client handouts ✅ Guidance for every stage of the visit, from pre-visit prep to post-visit follow-up ✅ Help with reading feline behavior, gentler handling, and coaching cat owners Its worth the effort.
L64: A 2023 Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery study compared 320 Cat Friendly practices with more than 4,100 conventional clinics. The Cat Friendly practices saw cats more often, ran diagnostic tests at 12% more visits, and found more clinically relevant issues, including endocrine and renal disease.

L84: 【60†Bryan Johnson】 is extending his biohacking approach to his dog, and I think there's a real reason for it. He adopted a Belgian Malinois named Katara in August, citing research showing dog owners have about a 24 percent lower relative risk of death, though that evidence is observational- a correlation, not proof. He now wants to apply his longevity approach to her, starting with her diet and discussing potential anti-aging therapies including medications.
L85: He argues that veterinary drug development moves faster than human trials, while dogs still share enough biology with us to yield informative results. Companies like Loyal are already pursuing FDA approval for canine longevity drugs for that exact reason, and while their programs have cleared major efficacy milestones and at least one safety submission, they haven't received confirmed full approval yet.
L86: Johnson revealed he had lived with unexplained low ferritin for about eleven years, without anemia, before blood work, an endoscopy, and stomach biopsies led to an autoimmune gastritis diagnosis, with his hemoglobin staying normal enough for the low ferritin to go unrecognized for years despite the extensive monitoring his Blueprint protocol is known for. I think the data itself held up fine; the real gap was in how it got read.
L87: Whether the subject is a person or now a dog, more tracking only helps if someone is targeting the right variables and following an unexplained signal instead of treating the rest of the numbers as reassurance. Do you think canine trials are a legitimate way to accelerate longevity research, or does treating a dog as a data set say something else about where this space is headed?

L101: We talk a lot about the free veterinary care already happening inside these walls on a smaller scale, vaccines, microchips, prevention, minor medical concerns, medications, education, and about everything we will be able to add once the clinic is fully equipped and operational. Obviously, providing free veterinary care to Gary families is a huge part of why we are building this. But there is another piece of this clinic that I don’t think we talk about nearly enough.
L102: Who gets to imagine themselves working inside those walls someday? We don’t just want children in Gary to grow up knowing there is a veterinary clinic in their community. We want them to know there could be a place for them in veterinary medicine, too. The clinic will also create a veterinary career pathway for local youth through education, curriculum, volunteering, shadowing, and hands-on exposure to veterinary medicine. In a community that is approximately 90% BIPOC, representation and exposure matter.
L103: We want young people in Gary to walk into a veterinary clinic in their own community, meet veterinary professionals who may look like them, participate in the work, and begin imagining themselves on the other side of the exam table someday. For some, it may be their first opportunity to discover that careers in veterinary medicine even exist or to see one as attainable for them.
L104: Our long-term vision therefore addresses both sides of veterinary access: who can receive veterinary care today and who has the opportunity to become part of the profession tomorrow. As this model grows, we hope Gary can become not only a community where veterinary access inequities are being addressed, but a place other communities can look to when developing solutions of their own.
L105: Maybe a child walks through our doors because their dog needs a vaccine and walks out thinking, “I could do this someday.” That’s part of what we’re building, too. In Gary. With Gary. For Gary. 🩶

L121: One day, one of my colleagues was wondering aloud what she and other veterinary clinicians around her who often did rectal palpations, abdominal surgeries, and tubed and administered antibiotics to hospitalized large animals might be carrying in terms of antimicrobial resistant pathogens. From that question came the STRIVE study - STudying Resistance In Veterinary Environments.
L122: We sampled workers from our veterinary hospital - clinicians, nurses, research staff, admin - and veterinary personnel from a small number of small animal hospitals in the greater Philadelphia area and characterized what kind of AMR pathogens they carried and how expansive their resistome was.
L123: The result was this publication! 【78†https://lnkd.in/ek-CHp-r】 Takeaways: - Vet personnel carries MRSA at much higher rates than the general population, and carriage was associated with having administered antibiotics to patients - The workplace environment had a small, subtle effect on the microbiome - Personnel working with patients had slightly higher levels of antimicrobial resistance genes that confer resistance to some of the more commonly used antibiotics at the hospital (tet(T) and dfrF, associated with resistance to tetracyclines and trimethoprim).
L124: 【79†Antimicrobial-resistant organism carriage and metagenomic characterization of the microbiome and resistome in veterinary workers - Veterinary Research Communications link.springer.com】

L22: The UC Davis Weill School of Veterinary Medicine is recruiting dogs with suspected or confirmed glioma for two clinical trials exploring new approaches to diagnosis, treatment, and disease monitoring. The CARE Trial is investigating an experimental drug in combination with radiation therapy. The PRISM Trial offers radiation therapy and observational/palliative pathways while studying the relationship between clinical signs, disease progression and tumor biology.
L23: Together, these studies aim to improve our understanding of canine glioma and its molecular characteristics, with potential implications for both veterinary and human medicine. 🔗 Learn more and see if your dog may be eligible: 【12†https://lnkd.in/gdn2AuNF】 Financial support is available toward eligible diagnostic and treatment costs, and participating dogs are monitored by the UC Davis veterinary neuro-oncology team. Participation does not guarantee an improved outcome.
L24: Eligibility is determined by the clinical trial team. 【13†#VeterinaryClinicalTrials】 | 【14†#CanineCancer】 | 【15†#Glioma】 Image description: A dog enrolled in a UC Davis clinical trial for canine glioma alongside members of the veterinary research team. L33: A canine patient named Frank is helping Purdue researchers study the biological effects of High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound, or HIFU, in appendicular osteosarcoma. After being diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma, Frank enrolled in Purdue Veterinary Medicine’s HIFU Osteosarcoma Clinical Trial. The study is evaluating the safety, feasibility and biological effects of HIFU in dogs newly diagnosed with the disease.
L34: As part of the study, researchers treated a portion of Frank’s tumor with HIFU before his standard-of-care limb amputation. Advanced imaging and tumor samples collected before and after treatment are being used to examine how HIFU affects tumor tissue and the surrounding environment, including potential changes in immune response. Frank subsequently continued his cancer care with chemotherapy and follow-up visits through Purdue University Veterinary Hospital’s Oncology Service.
L35: He has completed his planned treatments and is currently in remission. The HIFU Osteosarcoma Clinical Trial is currently enrolling dogs who meet study criteria, including a diagnosis of appendicular osteosarcoma with no evidence of metastatic disease. Visit the link in our comment for study and enrollment information. We are grateful to Frank and his family for their participation in this research.

L44: 🔬 What do you do when a 2-day-old foal with neonatal sepsis isn't responding to standard treatment? At 【24†Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine】, the answer was to try something that had never been done before in a septic neonatal foal. A new case report recently published in the Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine describes the first use of polymer-based extracorporeal hemoperfusion (HP) in a septic neonatal foal.
L45: A 2-day-old Miniature Horse filly presented in critical condition at 【25†Cornell Equine】 Hospital. When conventional therapy failed to bring improvement within 24 hours, the team implemented hemoperfusion using the 【26†VetResQ】 device to remove inflammatory cytokines and other harmful compounds from the blood.
L46: The treatment was well tolerated and was associated with improved physical examination findings and reduced cytokine concentrations - offering important proof-of-concept even in the face of a heartbreaking outcome. This case is part of a broader program at Cornell, where a team led by Dr. 【27†Barbara Delvescovo】 and Dr. 【28†Jethro Forbes, DVM, DACVECC】 in collaboration with Dr.
L47: 【29†Kallie Hobbs】 at 【30†Texas A&M University】 is pioneering the clinical and research application of hemoperfusion in large animal medicine. From sepsis and endotoxemia to selected toxicities, the goal is to bring advanced blood purification therapies to equine patients who need them most.
L48: Congratulations to the full team on this publication: 【31†Hanna Sfraga】, 【28†Jethro Forbes, DVM, DACVECC】, 【29†Kallie Hobbs】, Marta Cercone, Elizabeth Williams Louie, Jamie Lemus, 【32†Gillian Perkins】, and 【27†Barbara Delvescovo】.

L72: 🔬 Canine oncology is moving upstream, and the commercial map has not caught up yet. Veterinary Practice News reports that AI-assisted cytology tools are being integrated into general practice workflows, improving speed and confidence in early cancer detection in dogs without requiring specialist referral. The editorial frames AI as a decision-support layer, not a replacement for clinical judgment. That framing matters commercially.
L73: Earlier detection at the general practice level shifts the treatment initiation point upstream. Products that are currently positioned for confirmed or advanced disease may now have a credible role in newly diagnosed or at-risk patients before referral. Brand teams in oncology and diagnostics should be mapping where their product fits in a world where a general practitioner, aided by AI cytology interpretation, is making earlier calls with greater confidence.
L74: The question is not whether AI will change the detection window. It already is. The question is which brands have repositioned their commercial messaging to meet the earlier initiation point before their competitors do. 🐕 【14†#caninecancer】 【18†#veterinaryoncology】 【53†#companionanimalhealth】 【54†#veterinarydiagnostics】 【55†#animalhealthcommercial】

L104: When faced with a death occurring during the perioperative period, we ask ourselves: “Would this patient still be alive if they had not been anaesthetised?” 🐶🐱💉 That’s a big question -one that, in many cases, we still can’t answer. But we can get better at assessing the role anaesthesia may have played in a death. For decades, studies have used very different criteria. Some only consider deaths that occur during anaesthesia. Others look at the first 24 or 48 hours, while some extend the period to 15 days.
L105: Some include sedation; others don’t. And the criteria used to determine the role of anaesthesia also vary. So we’re not always measuring the same thing. And if we’re not measuring the same thing, how can we compare results, identify risk factors and improve anaesthetic safety? That’s why D.R.E.A.M. 💭 was born: Definition Research for Establishing Anaesthetic Mortality.
L106: And now, we’re very happy to share that our consensus study on defining and classifying peri-anaesthetic mortality in dogs and cats has just been published in BMC Veterinary Research. 🎉 This work is part of my research at 【66†Universidad CEU Cardenal Herrera†es.linkedin.com】, and it’s only the beginning. Our next step is to turn this consensus into a structured tool that can help us assess real cases more objectively and reproducibly.
L107: A huge thank you to the 47 experts who took part, for their commitment and for believing in this project ♥️, and a very special thank you to 【67†Nacho Redondo García†es.linkedin.com】, my PhD supervisor, for his constant support and for everything he continues to teach me along the way.
